title: Koh Samui Transportation Guide: Getting Around the Island in 2026
description: From Grab taxis to scooters and songthaews, this Koh Samui transportation guide tells you exactly how to get around the island affordably and safely.

blocks.text: Getting around Koh Samui is one of the first practical questions every visitor faces. The island has no public bus system, but a mix of options — songthaews, metered taxis, Grab, rental scooters, and private drivers — means you’re never stranded. Here’s how to navigate Koh Samui transport like a local.

Songthaews are shared pick-up trucks with bench seating in the back. They circulate the island’s ring road in both directions and are the closest thing Koh Samui has to a public bus. The standard fare is 50–80 THB per person for most routes. Flag one down on the main road, tell the driver your destination, and he’ll nod if he’s going your way. They run roughly 6 am to 9 pm — don’t rely on them late at night.

Grab (Southeast Asia’s Uber equivalent) is widely available on Koh Samui and is the most transparent way to get a quoted price before you commit. Coverage is strong in the main areas: Chaweng, Lamai, Bophut, Bangrak, Choeng Mon, and Plai Laem. In more remote parts of the island, wait times can be longer. Set up the app before you leave home.

Koh Samui’s local taxis are not metered — fares are fixed by the driver and can vary wildly. Always agree on the price before getting in. The standard Chaweng to airport fare runs 200–300 THB; cross-island trips to the west coast can reach 600–800 THB. Having a Grab alternative on your phone gives you instant leverage in negotiations.

Renting a scooter is the most popular way to explore Koh Samui independently. Daily rates run 200–350 THB for an automatic 110–125 cc bike, or 400–600 THB for a larger manual motorbike. Rental shops are everywhere — bring your licence (an international driving permit is technically required), always wear a helmet, and carry your passport copy.
The ring road is manageable, but hillside roads in areas like Plai Laem and the interior can be steep and slippery after rain. Ride with extra caution.

Self-drive car hire is available through international companies at the airport and local operators in Chaweng. Rates start around 1,000–1,500 THB per day. Driving in Thailand is on the left. Having a car is genuinely useful for families or groups doing cross-island excursions.

Many villas — especially in the north of the island around Plai Laem and Choeng Mon — arrange private airport transfers as part of the stay. Book in advance, as Koh Samui Airport can be chaotic on arrival. A private transfer from the airport to the Plai Laem area costs approximately 400–600 THB and takes 15–25 minutes depending on traffic.

For day trips to Ang Thong Marine Park, Koh Phangan, or Koh Tao, the main departure points are Bangrak Pier (Big Buddha Pier) in the north and Don Sak Pier (via the mainland). Bangrak is 5 minutes from the Plai Laem area — one of the most convenient locations on the island for ferry access.

Unlike the mainland, Koh Samui’s tuk-tuks are more of a novelty than a primary transport mode. You’ll find them in tourist areas, mainly for short hops. Prices are negotiable but tend to be higher than songthaews for the same distance.
